body.heading: Shah mat: the king is dead
paragraphs: Chess grew from an Indian game, travelled through Persia, and reached Europe carrying Persian words in its luggage. When a king was attacked, Persian players announced “shah” — king — which reached English as “check”.

The finishing word, checkmate, comes from the Persian phrase “shah mat”, usually explained as “the king is dead” or “the king is helpless”. Either way, the meaning is the same: the king has no escape, and the game is over.

body.heading: A board full of borrowed words
paragraphs: The rook is another traveller: its name comes from the Persian “rukh”, meaning chariot, which is why the piece originally represented a war chariot rather than a castle tower. The castle shape came later, as the word changed in European mouths.
Even “pawn” has a story — it comes through French from a Latin word for a foot soldier. The humblest piece on the board carries the oldest job description in the army.

body.heading: Try it: word origins at the board
paragraphs: Next time you play, announce your checks in the old style: “Shah!” It adds a thousand years of drama to a Tuesday-evening game. Then look at the pieces and ask which other names might be hiding a journey.

For a research race, pick five everyday words — pyjamas, ketchup, algebra, coffee, shampoo — and guess each one's home language before checking. Chess is not the only traveller in the dictionary; it is just the one with the best stories.

takeaway: Checkmate is a Persian sentence wearing English clothes: every time you say it, you announce the fate of a king.
